Maladaptive Strategies.value: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
I can no longer trust my own body
The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat items 'Checking Behind' and 'Back to Wall' imply a persistent interpersonal pursuit/assault-style danger (someone following me, needing surveillance of the room) that is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless there is additional trauma content not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Institutional Failure' is not a natural fit with the rest of this MVC profile: the other items center on fragmented accident memory, mistrust of self/body, and hypervigilance, but this appraisal presupposes a salient protector/institution betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type or other selected items.

issues.item: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' does not connect well to the represented triggers, memory, or appraisals. For an MVC case, avoidance is more coherently focused on travel, roads, vehicles, reminders of the crash, or internal trauma cues; avoidance of prior social contacts suggests a different maintaining process that is not otherwise represented.

vignette:
At sixty-eight years old, Kofi found himself grappling with a tumultuous inner world that had been irrevocably altered by a life-threatening motor vehicle collision six months earlier. Once a passionate dancer who filled studios with movement and laughter, Kofi now felt as if he were moving through a fog, each day a struggle to navigate the remnants of a life that had once been vibrant. The accident had left him with a fractured sense of safety; he could almost hear the screech of tires and the crunch of metal every time he closed his eyes. The memory was a jigsaw puzzle with too many pieces missing, and he felt like he was floating in the space between what was and what might never be again.

The day of the accident replayed in fragments, images flickering like a faulty reel in his mind. He remembered the warmth of the sun on his skin as he crossed the street, the laughter of fellow dancers in the distance, and then, abruptly, the chaos that ensued. The blaring horn, the sudden impact, and a rush of adrenaline as he fought for consciousness. But when he tried to piece together the events, Kofi found the story elusive, like trying to catch smoke with his bare hands. What frightened him most was not just the memory itself but the incomplete picture; he felt he was missing something crucial, something that might clarify the narrative of his life.

In the months that followed the accident, Kofi's world shrank. He avoided going out, the thought of stepping outside felt insurmountable. The once-familiar streets of his neighborhood transformed into a landscape of potential dangers. He avoided social contacts, too, shying away from friends and fellow dancers who had once been his support system. He couldn’t bear to see the concern in their eyes or the awkwardness that followed him like a shadow. Each time he thought about attending a gathering, a tight knot formed in his stomach, reminding him of the chaos he had endured. Instead, he found himself retreating into the confines of his small apartment, where the familiar walls could offer a semblance of safety. But even there, he felt the need to position himself with his back against the wall, eyes scanning the room for any sign of threat. This habit developed into a ritual of sorts; he would only feel secure if he could see everyone, as though that visibility would grant him some control over the unpredictable world outside.

His heightened sense of threat transformed the simplest sounds into harbingers of doom. A loud clap of thunder or a sudden burst of laughter from outside sent him spiraling into panic. Kofi would jump, heart racing, convinced that something terrible was about to unfold. Delays in his daily routine also triggered his anxiety; if the kettle took too long to boil, he would wonder if it was a sign of something worse to come. He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, one where he could no longer trust his own body to react appropriately in moments of crisis. The once fluid movements he displayed as a dancer were now marred by a creeping self-doubt that lingered like a specter. He questioned whether he would be able to dance again, to trust that his legs would carry him without faltering. 

This fear was compounded by the sense of betrayal he felt from the very institutions meant to safeguard him. Kofi was left with the nagging thought that the drivers, the paramedics, and the medical teams had all failed him in some way. What should have been a network of support felt instead like a web of institutional failure, leaving him feeling more isolated and vulnerable than ever. Every interaction with a healthcare professional became tinged with suspicion, as if they were judging him or dismissing his pain. 

As he sat in the dim light of his living room one evening, the weight of his symptoms pressing down on him, Kofi finally recognized that he could no longer navigate this storm alone. He had spent months pushing thoughts of therapy aside, convinced that confronting his trauma would only deepen his wounds. Yet, the isolation was becoming unbearable; he missed the connection of others, the warmth of shared experience. What he hoped for most now was a pathway back to himself, a way to reclaim the joy he had once found in dance and community. With a trembling resolve, Kofi picked up the phone to seek help, fearing what he might uncover but also yearning for the possibility of healing.
